title: Why Classroom Language Matters
brief: Introduce the idea that the language a teacher uses to run the room is a distinct skill separate from teaching content. Draw on the source's repeated framing of 'giving clear instructions' as a named classroom management topic worthy of deliberate attention, and on the observation that teachers use 'phrases and techniques' to control discussion and maintain order. Explain that unclear or over-complicated teacher talk creates off-task behaviour — students standing when they should be sitting, not following directions, or talking out of turn — and that this unit focuses on the teacher's own language as the primary tool for preventing those moments.

title: Grading Your Language for the Room
brief: Cover the principle of matching the complexity of your spoken language to what learners can process, drawing on the source's example of a teacher who maintains two versions of an agenda — one a simple list and one a detailed narrative — so that different proficiency levels can access the same information. Use the source's note-taking abbreviation examples (T = teacher, Ss = students, TL = target language) to illustrate how even professional observers strip language down to its essentials, and connect that economy of words to the kind of short, clear language a teacher should aim for when addressing the class. Exclude discussion of vocabulary teaching activities, which belong to other units.

title: Giving Short, Clear Instructions
brief: Focus on the practical craft of constructing a clean instruction, using the source's explicit identification of 'Giving Clear Instructions' as a discussion and reflection topic. Draw on the source's description of a teacher who asks students to repeat directions back, asks students whether they understand what they need to do, and uses gestures to convey meaning — presenting these as three concrete techniques. Provide before-and-after examples contrasting a muddled multi-clause instruction with a stripped-down version that delivers one action at a time, using the source's own abbreviated observation language as a model for the kind of directness teachers should aim for.

title: Demonstrating Rather Than Explaining
brief: Explore the technique of showing students what to do instead of describing it in words, drawing on the source's references to teachers using gestures to attract attention, gestures to convey meaning, and physical movement as a classroom management and communication tool. Use the source's observation that a teacher 'gestures to attract the students' attention' before giving a summary instruction as a concrete example of non-verbal demonstration replacing verbal explanation. Connect this to the broader principle that when words are reduced and actions are increased, comprehension improves — particularly for very young learners who have short attention spans and find it hard to sit still and process long verbal explanations.

title: Checking Instructions Were Understood
brief: Cover the specific moves a teacher can make after giving an instruction to verify that students have understood it, drawing directly on the source's description of a teacher who checks student comprehension of directions, asks students to repeat the directions, and asks students if they understand what they need to do. Distinguish these comprehension-checking moves from the broader topic of concept-checking questions used in vocabulary teaching, which is outside this unit's scope. Use the source's framing of 'Giving Instructions' as a named focus question — 'How does the teacher check that students understand the directions for the first warm-up activity?' — to anchor the discussion and give trainees a clear observational lens.

title: Putting It Together: Muddled vs Clean Instructions
brief: Consolidate the unit by presenting extended before-and-after examples that contrast muddled instructions with clean ones, drawing on the source's identification of common off-task behaviours — students not following directions, standing when they should be sitting, talking out of turn — as symptoms of unclear teacher language. Use the source's observation that teachers need techniques to manage off-task students 'without disrupting the flow of the lesson' to frame clean instructions as a proactive rather than reactive strategy. Walk through a short sequence showing how grading language, demonstrating the task, and checking understanding work together as a routine, and invite trainees to reflect on whether they could adapt these techniques for their own teaching contexts.
